pages.text: Wires are strung between $(item)insulators$(), $(item)transformers$() and $(item)power pylons$(). Put an insulator on a machine or cable, take a $(item)wire coil$(), $(thing)use$() it on the first insulator and then on the second. The wire sags and must not pass through blocks. Each connection uses one coil.

$(l)Copper$(): 2,048 FE/t, up to 16 blocks. $(l)Steel$(): 16,384 FE/t, up to 24 blocks, lower loss. $(l)High-voltage$(): 131,072 FE/t, up to 48 blocks, almost lossless; only on high-voltage insulators, the transformer top and pylons. High voltage only runs from generators to transformers: a high-voltage insulator works only on a generator, power plant, transformer or bus duct, never on a machine. Loss grows with length.$(br2)$(4)Overload:$() if more energy goes through a wire in one tick than it can carry, it $(l)burns out$() with sparks and smoke and is gone, e.g. copper wire between two steel insulators on a strong line.$(br2)$(4)Shock:$() wires are bare. Touching a wire that carries power hurts: copper 1 heart, steel 2.5, high voltage 6 hearts, sets on fire and throws back. Dead wires are safe.

The $(item)transformer$() stores 20,000,000 FE. The front bushing takes copper and steel wire (up to 16,384 FE/t), the top one high-voltage wire (up to 131,072 FE/t). At the front it steps power down: a $(item)bus duct$() gets up to 524,288 FE/t, cables and machines what they carry and takes it on the other sides except the top. Power only flows to emptier stores.
The $(item)power pylon$() is an 8-block tower with two cross-arms and four insulator strings. It takes steel and high-voltage wire; the wires run along the direction you faced when placing it.
